Social isolation, social support, and treatment outcomes in post-traumatic stress disorder.
This observational cohort study followed adults with PTSD and examined how perceived social isolation
and social support predicted response to trauma-focused treatment. Greater social isolation at baseline
was associated with smaller symptom improvement and higher dropout, while stronger social support
predicted better outcomes and sustained remission. The authors argue that support interventions,
peer groups, and family involvement should be considered alongside evidence-based psychotherapy for
isolated patients. Mechanistic background research on loneliness and threat processing is discussed as
context, but the study notes this is not direct evidence for any specific treatment. Limitations include
reliance on self-report measures of isolation, a predominantly civilian sample, and possible confounding
by depression severity and unemployment.
